claims.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the global energy crisis.
claims.reasoning: Russia's invasion of Ukraine (February 24, 2022) and its role in exacerbating the global energy crisis is a widely documented and confirmed fact, particularly affecting European natural gas supplies.

claims.text: Countries are not on track to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, the conservative figure established by the Paris Agreement, per the IPCC report.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 WGIII report (April 4, 2022) confirmed that countries' current pledges and policies are insufficient to limit warming to 1.5°C. The 1.5°C target is correctly described as the more conservative Paris Agreement threshold (the agreement also references a 2°C limit).

claims.text: Global emissions will need to peak by 2030 at the latest, and then steeply reduce thereafter, to prevent worsening impacts.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 WGIII report explicitly states that global greenhouse gas emissions must peak 'before 2025 at the latest' — not by 2030. This is the article's single falsified claim. The 2030 figure in the report refers to the required 43% emissions reduction from 2019 levels by 2030 after the peak, not the peak deadline itself.

claims.text: Fossil fuel infrastructure must be abandoned, including coal assets by 2030 and oil and gas by around 2050.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 WGIII report's findings on coal phase-out by 2030 and oil and gas phase-down by ~2050 are consistent with the reported findings. The report called for abandonment of unabated coal by 2030 (for developed nations) as part of 1.5°C-compatible pathways.

claims.text: U.N. Secretary General Antonio Guterres described new fossil fuel infrastructure investment as 'moral and economic madness.'
claims.reasoning: Guterres' 'moral and economic madness' quote in reference to new fossil fuel infrastructure investment is a widely documented statement made at the April 4, 2022 press conference accompanying the IPCC WGIII report release.

claims.text: IPCC reports are approved by all 195 countries that signed the Paris Agreement; the latest report was compiled by 278 authors from 65 countries.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 WGIII Summary for Policymakers was approved by 195 IPCC member governments. The report was compiled by 278 authors from 65 countries. These figures are confirmed in the official IPCC press release and briefings.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: Seth Borenstein is the real Associated Press science reporter who covered the IPCC AR6 WGIII report. The apnews.com domain is AP's real news website domain. This contact is real.
The IPCC is the real UN body for assessing climate science. Its AR6 Working Group III report on mitigation was released April 4, 2022.

claims.text: PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are a group of approximately 12,000 chemicals used in industrial and consumer products such as nonstick pans, food packaging and firefighting foam.
claims.reasoning: Multiple authoritative sources confirm there are more than 12,000 types of PFAS chemicals. The EPA, USGS, and others consistently use this figure.

claims.text: An ABC News analysis found that 43% of U.S. ZIP codes have had at least one water source where PFAS contamination was detected over the past 20 years.
claims.reasoning: The ABC News data analysis finding of 43% of U.S. ZIP codes with detected PFAS contamination is consistent with federal data. A USGS study found approximately 45% of the nation's tap water has one or more PFAS, closely consistent with the 43% ZIP code figure.

claims.text: New PFAS detections in water sources each year rose from 753 in 2013 to 2,321 in 2021, with at least 143 million Americans possibly drinking contaminated tap water.
claims.reasoning: These figures come from the ABC News data analysis of federal and state environmental agency data. The 143 million Americans figure is consistent with independent estimates — NRDC and other organizations have cited comparable figures for PFAS exposure.

claims.text: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine put out medical guidelines suggesting that people whose blood contains PFAS above 2 nanograms per milliliter should get additional screening for high cholesterol, cancer and other health risks.
claims.reasoning: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine released PFAS health guidelines in 2022 recommending additional clinical follow-up for persons with PFAS blood levels above 2 ng/mL. This is confirmed in the NASEM report and widely cited in news coverage.

claims.text: The EPA proposed the first federal limits on six forever chemicals and microplastics in drinking water, setting a limit of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS.
claims.reasoning: The EPA's March 2023 proposal (and April 2024 final rule) established limits on six PFAS chemicals — PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA (GenX), and PFBS. WASHINGTON (AP) — An analysis finds a critical group of U.S. employers would face a direct cost of $82.3 billion from President Donald Trump’s current tariff plans[source article excerpt omitted].

The findings show clear trade-offs from Trump’s import taxes, contradicting his claims foreign manufacturers would absorb the costs of the tariffs instead of U.S. companies that rely on imports. While the tariffs launched under Trump have yet to boost overall inflation[source article excerpt omitted].

Had the initial April 2 tariffs stayed in place, the companies in the JPMorganChase Institute analysis would’ve faced additional direct costs of $187.6 billion. Under the current rates, the $82.3 billion would be equivalent on average to $2,080 per employee, or 3.1% of the average annual payroll.

There’s a growing body of evidence suggesting more inflation could surface. The investment bank Goldman Sachs said in a report it expects companies to pass 90% of their tariff costs onto consumers. The Atlanta Federal Reserve has used its survey of businesses’ inflation expectations to say companies could on average pass along roughly half their costs from a 10% tariff or a 25% tariff without reducing consumer demand.

[source article excerpt omitted]. Kennedy, a leading antivaccine activist before becoming the nation’s top health official, has made or proposed numerous changes to the nation’s vaccine system, including firing the entire 17-member panel earlier this year and replacing it with a group that includes several anti-vaccine voices.

Discussions on the MMRV vaccine focused largely on rare instances of feverish seizures associated with the first dose, given to kids between ages 1 and 2. The panel last dealt with the issue in 2009, when it said either the combination shot or separate MMR and chickenpox shots were acceptable for the first dose, but that separate doses were generally preferred. Today, 85% of kids receive the combination dose for the first round, according to information presented at the meeting.

The group voted 8-1, with three abstentions, to keep MMRV covered for kids as young as 12 months under the Vaccines for Children program, which pays for about half the shots given to kids in the U.S.

As many as 2.4 million people in U.S. are estimated to have hepatitis B, which can cause serious liver infections. A hepatitis B vaccine was first licensed in the U.S. in 1981. In 2005, the ACIP recommended a dose within 24 hours of birth for all medically stable infants who weigh at least 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). Following the 2005 recommendation, hepatitis B cases among infants fell from 5,494 cases per year in 2005 to 2,214 cases in 2023.

Ungar reported from Louisville, Kentucky. AP Medical Writer Lauran Neergaard contributed to this story.
